images.title: "Prairie Avenue Improvement. Some of the Notable Sales and Improvements on That Street During the Last Few Months."
images.creator: Chicago Sunday Tribune (real-estate section)
images.repository: Internet Archive (Chicago Tribune microfilm, pub_chicago-daily-tribune)
images.collection: The Chicago Sunday Tribune, Nov. 10, 1901 (vol. 60 no. 313), real-estate page
images.found_via: IA full-text search '"1612 prairie"'; article read on the page image (IIIF crops) — the OCR drops the Frost & Granger and McKinlock lines
images.notes: A street-wide round-up written two and a half years before the target date — the closest thing to a 1904 inventory of changes. For the thin north-half houses: (1612) "Charles E. Brown is about completing his improvements and alterations, through Frost & Granger, on the Studebaker residence, 1612 Prairie avenue" — so the 1904 form of 1612 is the 1901 Frost & Granger remodel of the Studebaker house, not the 1869 original (new architect for the library). (1709) "Jesse Spalding has greatly improved the old Palmer Kellogg residence at 1709 and is now occupying it as his permanent home" — the Kellogg house stood, remodelled, and in 1904 was presumably the Spalding home (cf. Spalding at 1637 earlier). (1702 → 1700/1706) "On the site of the old Harvey residence at 1702, J. J. Glessner is building two modern colonial brick houses, after plans by Shepley, Rutan & Coolidge. It is understood that Mr. Glessner's son and daughter will occupy these when completed" — confirms the 1702 house was gone by late 1901 and the townhouses were brick, colonial, under construction in Nov. 1901. Also: Wirt Dexter property (1721) sold to a Spalding with the condition that the purchaser "must either build anew or move back the present brick residence to conform with the building lines now existing"; George A. McKinlock settled in the old Sturges residence at 1712; Stanley Field bought O. R. Keith's 1808; Lowden 'greatly embellished' the M. T. Greene house at 1912; Robbins bought the Hamill house at 2126 for 'extensive alterations'; Byron L. Smith 'completely remodeled the interior' at 2140.
images.rights_basis: Published in the United States before 1929

images.notes: Construction photo by George Glessner: the brick shell of the Shepley, Rutan & Coolidge townhouses with slate mansard and pedimented dormers in place, window openings still unglazed, a builder's shed and lumber in the front yard; stone string course, keystoned first-floor arches and a sign board over the door. At left a three-storey brick/stone house with a two-storey bay and a hooded doorway (= 1708, the house immediately south; Thorne residence by 1911 — see the Christmas-tree photograph captioned 1708/1706/1700; 1911 Sanborn: 1708 3-storey brick dwelling); at right the steep-gabled Gothic Revival house with porch (1638, Gregory — the 1600 and 1700 blocks were not separated by a through 17th Street). Gives the exact massing and materials (red brick, light stone trim) of the pair as finished c.1902 and shows the neighbours in 1901.

images.notes: The Shepley, Rutan & Coolidge Georgian Revival double townhouse built 1901–02 for the Glessner children: a continuous three-storey dark-brick block under a slate mansard with pedimented dormers and a wooden roof balustrade (Chinese-Chippendale pattern); stone keystoned flat-arched windows on the second floor, round-arched first-floor windows with iron balconettes; two mirror-image columned entrance porticoes with balconies above, at the outer ends; iron area railings. At the right edge the steep-gabled Gothic Revival house with pointed windows = 1638 (Gregory), immediately north — the 1600 and 1700 blocks were continuous (no through 17th Street; see the atlas crop record). At left a rusticated stone-trimmed three-storey neighbour = 1708 (James Ward Thorne residence by 1911; cf. the 'Christmas tree' photograph, which captions the same three houses as 1708, 1706, 1700). Caption labels left = 1706, right = 1700 (north unit), consistent with a view from the east. The same photograph appears (sepia, sharper) on the Glessner House blog post 'Kodak plant demolition begins' (2015-03-10) captioned 'Glessner townhouses, 1700-1706 S. Prairie Avenue, Shepley, Rutan & Coolidge, architects'. Strong evidence for the 1904 appearance; townhouses demolished 1954 for the Kodak plant expansion.

images.notes: The John W. Roberts Gothic Revival ('Hudson River Gothic') house: steep front gable with crocketed finial and oculus, paired pointed-arch windows with hood moulds, a canted ground-floor bay with pointed lights, a polygonal corner tower with pointed windows and a tall conical/pyramidal slate roof, a Gothic entrance porch with pierced brackets over a stoop, a lower wing at left, and gate piers with an iron fence. Thirty years before 1904 — use for persistence of lot treatments (fences, copings, lamp types), not for 1904 façades of rebuilt houses. Original journal holder not traced (lead: The Land Owner, 1869–1880s, CHM/Newberry runs). Same plate as a18-gh-landowner-1874-plate (Glessner House blog copy, link-only); this record carries the local full-sheet file. The Glessner House blog identifies the top-centre street vignette as 'Prairie Avenue looking southwest at 18th Street' (the pre-Glessner corner) — see a18-gh-landowner-1874-glessner-site; the vignette captioned 'Louis Wahl' is 2026 Prairie.

images.notes: Chicagology's per-address crop of the hand-coloured plate of Robinson's Atlas of the City of Chicago (E. Robinson, 1886) covering Prairie Avenue from 16th to 22nd Street (north at right; Indiana Avenue at top; the Illinois Central / Michigan Central tracks along the lake at lower right), with a black arrow added by Chicagology at the address. Plate conventions: pink = brick, yellow = frame, buff/brown = stone (a brown band at a pink front = stone front); X-crossed squares = rear stables on the alleys; frontage figures (ft) along the street line with the house numbers in small type below. All crops in this series are the same plate in two crop variants (3841×1482 and 3698×1400 px) and differ only by the arrow; the atlas itself is held by the Newberry (st-newberry-robinson-1886-atlas). Footprints are 1886 evidence — combine with the 1911 Sanborn for 1904. Rights: an 1886 atlas is public domain; the first-pass streams (a19/a20 Robinson crop records) treated these crops as link-only — this stream follows the pass instructions (dated published atlas → PD). Arrow points to sublots 37–38, west side: the brick double house of Hitchcock and Galloway (old 888/890) still standing in 1886 — the predecessor of the O. R. Keith house (Cobb & Frost, 1886).

images.notes: Two strips of flat front elevations drawn to a common scale. WEST SIDE (south→north, left→right): 1936 Allerton, 1912, 1906, 1900 Keith | 1834 Jones (two-storey with a mansard and central tower-dormer — consistent with the 1886 mansard addition), 1828 Shipman (small mansard), 1824 (large gabled stone front with bay — the Marsh refacing), 1816 Henderson (mansard with dormers), 1812 Wheeler (scrolled Flemish gable, round attic window), 1808 Keith (latticed parapet), 1800 Glessner (long, low, at far right). EAST SIDE (north→south, left→right as seen from the street): 1801 Kimball (château) with low service wing, 1811 Coleman (gable, arched entry), 1815 Sears/Meeker (mansard with gables), 1823 Dent (mansard), 1827 Doane (twin towers), then 1901, 1905 Field, 1919, 1923, 1945. Identification of each elevation is this researcher's reading from position and style (not captioned). Glessner House blog (2011, "Business Encroachment on Prairie Avenue") says the drawing "shows the 1800 and 1900 blocks of Prairie Avenue as they appeared at the time" of a 1914 Daily News article; author and date of the drawing are not stated — it looks like a modern reconstruction. The ONLY elevation-scale evidence found for 1816, 1823, 1824, 1828 and the post-1886 1834. Same drawing recorded by the 1900 stream from the blog (a19-gh-prairie-1800-1900-elevations). NOTE: the streetscape stream records the same chicagology image as st-chicagology-prairie-elevation-strips (no building ids); this record is kept for its per-house identification — merge the two.

Entrance hall at the NORTH end approached by New York brownstone steps sixteen feet wide; entrance hall 18½ x 12½ ft; octagonal main hall 30½ x 21 ft; stair hall 25 x 16 ft; galleried well 9 x 16 ft under a stained-glass dome; basement kitchen/laundry with steam from an engine and boilers "in the barn in the rear"; Edison incandescent lighting. Best dimensional source for 1827.

images.notes: Contemporary (1883–84) description of the house exterior and plan — the best period text for the 1904 model: 'red pressed brick, with trimmings of light sandstone, three stories in height, with main entrance in the center of the west front, at the head of a broad flight of granite steps, a high porte-cochère on the northern side, and a fine large conservatory on the southern. Stables and other out-buildings are in the rear, on the side nearest the lake'; 'spacious lawn and scattered shade-trees' on the south side; vestibule floored in varied marbles; main hall runs the entire depth ending at a winding stairway under a large stained-glass window; reception room (right of hall) with a window into the conservatory (fountain); drawing-room left of hall; library behind it with fireplace at the east end; dining room opposite, glass doors into the conservatory. Field lived here until his death in Jan 1906, so the exterior description should still apply in 1904 (porte-cochère/conservatory survival to 1904 to be checked against the 1911 Sanborn).

images.notes: Strip of five pen-and-ink entrance vignettes (3500×891 px), each labelled with its house number — the companion of the 1600/1620/1720/1726/1812 strip from the same article (a16-cgy-tribune-1898-prairie-widows). Shown on both the 1906 and 2035 pages. 1905 (Field): central double door under a bracketed portico with an iron-railed balcony, pedimented window at right, high straight stoop between square stone piers, scroll-pattern iron fence (matches the 1893 scroll fence; the tall-bar fence of c.1905 is later). 1906 (Edson Keith): three-storey Italianate front with a projecting full-height bay/tower at left under its own cornice, round-arched double door under a flat portico with balustraded balcony and arched window above, high stoop between stone cheek walls, balustraded terrace, arched hooded windows, tree at right — NB this does not match the mansard photograph Chicagology labels 1906 (a19-cgy-1906-keith-photo, which the 1900 stream identifies as 1900), supporting that identification. 1923 (Kellogg): mostly hidden by the big number cartouche — a wide arched entrance loggia with columns at the head of a long straight stoop, a bay at upper left, cornice, scroll iron fence and gate piers; the only individual depiction of 1923 found. 2035 (Mrs. H. O. Stone): a broad one-storey columned veranda across the front with an ornamental railing, entrance at left reached by a curving stair, tall round-arched upper windows, balustraded front fence — a detached house with a wide porch, not a narrow row-house front (relevant to the index's 'townhouse' entry for 2035). 2108 (Mark Kimball / M. T. Ames household): a rusticated/ashlar stone front, two tall round-arched windows on the parlour floor, round-arched doorway at right reached by a long straight stoop with plain rail, raised basement with barred arched windows, a domed or conical roof form of the neighbour at right — the first image of 2108; also evidence that 2108 was standing (cf. the 'empty lot' caption on cgs-2108-robinson-1886). images.notes: Yellow-mount stereo pair. The Van Osdel house as built: polychrome brick with light stone bands, a large round corner tower with bracketed cornice and FLAT top crowned by iron cresting, a second octagonal tower at the 22nd St. corner with mansard and cresting, Gothic dormers, Corinthian-columned entrance porch on Prairie with stone steps, low iron fence on stone curb, cast-iron gas lamp-post at the corner, young parkway tree, unpaved/macadam street. Period hand annotations on the left view: '22 St', 'Prairie Ave' and 'my room'(?) on the tower — from a resident or visitor. Confirms that the tall conical spires seen in a20-chicagology-2140-photo-a are a later alteration (B. L. Smith bought 1881; AIC index notes an 1881 remodeling). Downloaded from the Commons 1280-px thumbnail because upload.wikimedia.org rate-limited the original.

images.notes: Chicagology's per-address crop of the hand-coloured plate of Robinson's Atlas of the City of Chicago (E. Robinson, 1886) covering Prairie Avenue from 16th to 22nd Street (north at right; Indiana Avenue at top), full-resolution file (3698×1400 px) with a black arrow added by Chicagology. Plate conventions: pink = brick, yellow = frame, buff/brown = stone (a brown band at a pink front = stone front); X-crossed squares = rear stables on the alleys; frontage figures (ft) and small house numbers along the street lines. Every crop in the series is the same plate and differs only by the arrow; the first-pass aggregate records (a19-cgy-robinson-1886-crops-1900-block, a20-chicagology-robinson-1886-crops) and the Newberry atlas (st-newberry-robinson-1886-atlas) cover the plate as a whole — this record keeps the per-address crop because its arrow is Chicagology's lot identification, which the site plan can place by address. 1886 evidence only: combine with the 1911 Sanborn for 1904. Page caption: '2140 S. Prairie Ave. / Robinson Fire Insurance Map / 1886'. Arrow ends at the corner lots 8–9 at the north-west corner of 22nd Street: the Tucker (later B. L. Smith) house with its stable at the alley.

images.notes: Large clear photograph of the Van Osdel–designed Tucker/Byron L. Smith house on the NW corner of 22nd: dark brick with stone bands, three tall conical-roofed round/polygonal corner towers with cresting and finials, Gothic gabled dormers, clustered chimneys; tall iron picket fence on brick piers with ball finials; an iron-and-glass arched porte-cochère/entrance canopy on the 22nd Street (south) side. At right (north) a rough-faced stone house with a conical-roofed rounded bay — very probably 2130 Murdoch (H. I. Cobb, 1890) — and beyond it a long three-storey brick row. Overhead trolley wires and rails in 22nd Street, a cast-iron street lamp at right, a man with a bicycle. Strong 1904 evidence: shows the corner, the fence, the canopy and the trolley wires; date window inferred c. 1890–1911. Compared with the pre-1881 Greene stereograph, the towers here carry tall conical slate roofs — a later remodelling, after 1890 (the cresting-crowned towers still stood next to the 1890 Murdoch house in a20-glessner-vanosdel-2140-photo); whether 1904 had spires or cresting is unresolved — date this photo before choosing. The 1898 Van Osdel book plate (a20-aic-quarter-century-tucker-residence) still shows the cresting state, which (if the photo was current in 1898) would put the spires after 1898.

images.notes: Closer oblique of the same house showing richer original roof ornament: iron cresting crowns on the flat-topped towers, a tall spire/flèche, polychrome brick with stone string-courses, round tower with bracketed cornice, columned entrance porch on Prairie Avenue with stone stair, low iron fence on stone curb, gas lamp, hydrant and wooden tree guards. Comparison with a20-chicagology-2140-photo-a shows the tower tops changed (cresting crowns vs. tall conical roofs) — the conical roofs in photo A appear to be later; establish sequence before fixing 1904 roofline. The NYPL/P. B. Greene stereograph (pre-1881) shows the same cresting-crowned towers; the uncropped version (a20-glessner-vanosdel-2140-photo) shows the 1890 Murdoch house beside it, so this state lasted past 1890.

images.notes: Sepia photograph, a wider version of the image cropped on Chicagology (a20-chicagology-2140-photo-b): the Tucker/Smith house with flat-topped towers crowned by iron cresting, polychrome brick, columned Prairie Ave porch; AND at right the pale smooth-ashlar Murdoch house (H. I. Cobb, 1890) with its round bay/tower under a conical roof, plus a third house beyond — so this cresting-crowned state still existed after 1890. Blog text: built 1876 for W. F. Tucker by Van Osdel at the NW corner of 22nd St.; sold 1881 to Byron L. Smith (Northern Trust); razed 1936. The tall conical spires in a20-chicagology-2140-photo-a therefore date from a remodelling after 1890 — whether before or after 1904 is unresolved.

Right of centre the three-storey mansard double house (Hitchcock/Galloway); a smaller gabled cottage and a church-like tower further west along 18th St; plank sidewalks, picket fences, gas lamp. images.title: 1800 S. Prairie Ave. — Robinson Fire Insurance Map, 1886 [Chicagology address crop]
images.creator: E. Robinson (Robinson's Atlas of the City of Chicago, 1886); crop and arrow by Chicagology
images.repository: Chicagology (chicagology.com)
images.collection: Chicagology address pages; original: Robinson's Atlas of the City of Chicago (1886)
images.rights_basis: published 1886 (pre-1929, US); faithful reproduction via chicagology
images.found_via: chicagology Prairie Avenue index → per-address page (follow-up pass, all images on the page enumerated)
images.notes: Chicagology's per-address crop of the hand-coloured plate of Robinson's Atlas of the City of Chicago (E. Robinson, 1886) covering Prairie Avenue from 16th to 22nd Street (north at right; Indiana Avenue at top; the Illinois Central / Michigan Central tracks along the lake at lower right), with a black arrow added by Chicagology at the address. Plate conventions: pink = brick, yellow = frame, buff/brown = stone (a brown band at a pink front = stone front); X-crossed squares = rear stables on the alleys; frontage figures (ft) along the street line with the house numbers in small type below. All crops in this series are the same plate in two crop variants (3841×1482 and 3698×1400 px) and differ only by the arrow; the atlas itself is held by the Newberry (st-newberry-robinson-1886-atlas). Footprints are 1886 evidence — combine with the 1911 Sanborn for 1904. Rights: an 1886 atlas is public domain; the first-pass streams (a19/a20 Robinson crop records) treated these crops as link-only — this stream follows the pass instructions (dated published atlas → PD). Captioned "Proposed Site — John J. Glessner". Arrow ends at the corner lot (28-ft figure) at the SW corner of 18th and Prairie, which is EMPTY on the plate; the brick double house on the next lots south (labels 1808/1804) is still standing — the 1886 plate predates Glessner's construction (1886–87).

images.notes: Newly completed house from the north-east corner of Prairie and 18th: rough granite, the 18th Street front with its row of small windows, front arched entrance on Prairie, gas lamp post at the corner, fresh sidewalks and young trees, building debris and workmen still about. Plate conventions: pink = brick, yellow = frame, buff/brown = stone (a brown band at a pink front = stone front); X-crossed squares = rear stables on the alleys; frontage figures (ft) along the street line with the house numbers in small type below. All crops in this series are the same plate in two crop variants (3841×1482 and 3698×1400 px) and differ only by the arrow; the atlas itself is held by the Newberry (st-newberry-robinson-1886-atlas). Rights: an 1886 atlas is public domain; the first-pass streams (a19/a20 Robinson crop records) treated these crops as link-only — this stream follows the pass instructions (dated published atlas → PD). Plate conventions: pink = brick, yellow = frame, buff/brown = stone (a brown band at a pink front = stone front); X-crossed squares = rear stables on the alleys; frontage figures (ft) and small house numbers along the street lines. Every crop in the series is the same plate and differs only by the arrow; the first-pass aggregate records (a19-cgy-robinson-1886-crops-1900-block, a20-chicagology-robinson-1886-crops) and the Newberry atlas (st-newberry-robinson-1886-atlas) cover the plate as a whole — this record keeps the per-address crop because its arrow is Chicagology's lot identification, which the site plan can place by address. 1886 evidence only: combine with the 1911 Sanborn for 1904. Page caption: '1919 S. Prairie Ave. / Robinson Fire Insurance Map / 1886'. Arrow ends at the rear of lots 3–4 on the east side of the 1900 block: the plate prints 1919 over the narrow 40.25-ft lot 4, which holds a narrow brick house — the 1884 Murray house before the 1902 Field Jr. enlargement — with open ground (lot 3) between it and the Field house.

images.notes: Original form (read in OCR): 13-room two-storey frame house of rough-hewn oak, raised basement, 'Italian Victorian cupola, added after construction'; tall narrow main-floor windows, small 'eyebrow' windows upstairs; low-pitched front gable; 'originally … a typical Greek Revival columned portico'; moved 1872 by John Chrimes to 4526 S. Wabash; owner since 1941 St Paul Church of God in Christ. Bibliography lists Tribune 'The Clarke House: Henry B. Clarke's Ten Thousand Dollar House' (26 May 1872) and 'Discovery of Interesting Papers' (9 June 1872), plus 1939–1969 'oldest house' articles. 2000 amendment: footprint 42.44 × 47.37 ft, east facade, raised portico 31 × 9.5 ft (restored 1980 from a c.1855 daguerreotype in the Chicago Historical Society); HABS 1935 found most window mouldings, pilasters, shutters and the portico modified/removed; four corner pilasters, two roofline pediments and the cupola remained; neither the 1836 nor the 1872 foundation survives. Includes a site plan and floor plans of the house at 1827 S. Indiana (pp. 16–18) and a mid-20th-century photograph (p. 24). For 1904: the house stood at 4526 Wabash with cupola, no portico.

Robinson, 1886) covering Prairie Avenue from 16th to 22nd Street (north at right; Indiana Avenue at top), full-resolution file (3841×1482 px) with a black arrow added by Chicagology. Plate conventions: pink = brick, yellow = frame, buff/brown = stone (a brown band at a pink front = stone front); X-crossed squares = rear stables on the alleys; frontage figures (ft) and small house numbers along the street lines. Every crop in the series is the same plate and differs only by the arrow; the first-pass aggregate records (a19-cgy-robinson-1886-crops-1900-block, a20-chicagology-robinson-1886-crops) and the Newberry atlas (st-newberry-robinson-1886-atlas) cover the plate as a whole — this record keeps the per-address crop because its arrow is Chicagology's lot identification, which the site plan can place by address. 1886 evidence only: combine with the 1911 Sanborn for 1904. Arrow ends on the east side at the lot printed 2013 — the first Reid house, replaced in 1894 by the present Beers, Clay & Dutton house.

images.notes: Descriptions: Rees house (1888) — 'three stories and an attic … of Bedford stone that has been completely smoothed … on a rusticated base. A great, simple arch with over-sized voussoirs shelters the entrance. To its south, a curved bay stands two stories and ends in a semicircular copper roof. A group of five arched windows light the third floor and a steep gable with a single arched window rises to a finial.' Murdoch house (1890) — random ashlar of smooth stone on a battered foundation, corner porch on paired columns with trabeated openings, gable to the side yard, a semicircular-plan section rising to a conical roof above the third storey, low-relief frieze. ADDRESS CONFLICT: the older AIC page calls it 'Murdock … 2130 S. Calumet Ave., one block east of Prairie', the 1890–99 page '2130 S. Prairie'; Chicagology, the HMDB marker and the Robinson 1886 empty lot support Prairie. Also Gorton (2120 Prairie): Burnham & Root 1877 house for O. W. Clapp, Cobb music-room addition for F. S. Gorton (c.1891–96, demolished 1950). No Murdoch image in the catalogue; the only image found is as the neighbour in the 2140 photographs.

images.notes: 62-page PDF. Answers the 'HABS?' question: no HABS documentation is cited; the house is an NRHP individual listing (1999) and a Chicago Landmark (5 Feb 1998, per Wikipedia). Description: c.1870 three-storey Second Empire house of orange-rust brick (walls four courses thick) on an Indiana limestone raised basement, stone window hoods with incised floral ornament and large keystones, front (EAST) elevation in three zones; a limestone Queen Anne entry verandah/porch and front steps added c.1880–1900; a two-storey pressed-copper bay with pyramidal copper roof at the southeast corner added c.1880s–early 1890s (compared with the c.1890 copper bay on the Kimball house); alley to the west; a later warehouse/cooler addition at the NW. So in 1904 the house had its copper bay and stone porch (both pre-1904) but not the 20th-c. warehouse additions. Occupied by the Kohn family from 1874 for 34 years (to c.1908).

images.notes: Key text for the 1904 church. Lot 109'×171' at NW corner of Cullerton (20th) and Michigan; east & south facades of mottled bituminous ('fairy') limestone, north & west of Chicago common brick; gable roof; nave runs E–W with the parish house at right angles (abbreviated T); main entry on the east; balconies on E, N, S. Nave 95 ft long, 60 ft high, 75 ft wide incl. aisles. History: Renwick & Sands, completed 1874; spring 1900 fire gutted the nave; Shaw's rebuild completed 1901. EXTERIOR CHANGES MADE IN THE 1900–01 REBUILD (i.e. the 1904 state differs from Renwick's drawings): clerestory windows changed from pointed arches to a rectilinear grouping; the traditional rose window replaced by an ogee-shaped window; roof ridge LOWERED. Only later change: removal of the tower's hipped roof after storm damage in 1959 — so in 1904 the SE tower carried a hipped roof. Large Tiffany window over the main Michigan Avenue entry (4½ tons). Bibliography cites House Beautiful v.17 no.1 (Dec. 1904) — a contemporary illustrated article (lead).

images.notes: Most detailed account found of the church's EXTERIOR as it stood in 1904 (read in OCR). Cornerstone 21 Sept 1872; first services Jan 1873 (Sunday-school room) and 30 Nov 1873 (sanctuary); BELL TOWER COMPLETED 1884. 'The tower was originally topped by a graceful spire with a tall, slender finial, but these were lost due to wind damage in 1929' (the 1974 NRHP form instead says the tower's hipped roof was removed after a 1959 storm — conflict to resolve with dated photographs; either way the 1904 tower had a tall roof/spire). Church ~60 ft high; exterior 110 × 168 ft; nave about 72 × 116 ft; seats ~1,200. Fire of 9 March 1900 destroyed the roof and much of the nave interior; Shaw's rebuild LOWERED and flattened the nave roof (original 'more sharply pitched and its peak considerably higher'), and the east-wall rose window (La Farge round mosaic, destroyed 1900) was replaced. Exterior description: four-storey square tower with corner buttresses, open belfry with paired pointed arches and angel figures, corner gargoyles; central Gothic portal with head of Christ; five lancets and a large window under the gable with symbols of the Evangelists; north buttress pinnacle 'once topped by a tall finial'; north and south walls with three rows of windows (copper-framed opalescent clerestory, six large pointed windows, small windows below); north side brick; west transverse section with wheel window and copper oriel; mottled bituminous limestone laid in banded stringcourses. Original interior: tall Gothic arches on slender cast-iron columns, light and airy.

images.title: "Charles M. Henderson's Residence Partly Burned. Fire Breaks Out While All the Family but a Daughter Are at a Concert… Damage $10,000, Largely to Wardrobe…"
images.creator: Chicago Sunday Tribune (front page)

images.notes: Fire in the Henderson house 'shortly after 10 o'clock last night', damage about $10,000, 'nearly one-half' of it to Mrs. Henderson's wardrobe; pictures, tapestries and bric-a-brac damaged by the firemen. Miss Bessie Henderson was in her room on the SECOND FLOOR; four servant girls in another part of the house; the fire began on the lower floor. An interior fire with no structural loss reported — the house was repaired and the widow lived there until the 1920s (Tribune society notes 1896–1921; tax list July 4, 1903). So the 1873 Henderson house stood in 1904 with Mrs. C. M. Henderson as occupant; the library's 'unresolved' can be closed. Henderson died at 1816 on Jan. 23, 1896 and left the widow 'the homestead at No. 1816 Prairie avenue, the household furniture, and horses' (Tribune Feb. 8, 1896).

Robinson, 1886) covering Prairie Avenue from 16th to 22nd Street (north at right; Indiana Avenue at top), full-resolution file (3698×1400 px) with a black arrow added by Chicagology. Plate conventions: pink = brick, yellow = frame, buff/brown = stone (a brown band at a pink front = stone front); X-crossed squares = rear stables on the alleys; frontage figures (ft) and small house numbers along the street lines. images.notes: Built 1853 for John N. Staples, "Italian villa style", lake 250 ft to the east (page). Inter Ocean 18 Jun 1878: permit to Charles Busby, "three-story and basement addition to house at 854 Prairie avenue, to cost $12,000". Tribune 4 May 1879: two-storey barn at 854, $3,000. Inter Ocean 21 Nov 1879: fire "in the house of T. W. Harvey, 852 [sic] Prairie avenue… The building is a two-story brownstone front", damage $2,000. Sold 1880 to T. W. Harvey, who remodelled it; sold 1899 to John Glessner and razed (for the 1700/1706 townhouses). The Tribune 1898 calls it "the old Staples homestead, 1703 [sic] Prairie avenue".

images.notes: The 1853 John N. Staples house (first house on Prairie Ave): stuccoed/painted two-storey Italianate with low hipped roof, deep bracketed cornice, square glazed cupola/observatory, a two-storey wrap-around porch (turned columns, open balustraded upper deck), tall windows, a canted bay at right, lattice-skirted porch base and an ornate picket fence with turned balusters. Shows the house before Turlington W. Harvey's 1880 Second Empire remodelling; razed c.1899–1901 for the Glessner children's townhouses (1700/1706), so absent in 1904 — predecessor documentation only.

images.notes: KEY FIND FOR 1702 (thin building): the T. W. Harvey house after its 1880 remodelling — a Second Empire front with a slate mansard and pedimented dormers, a two-storey canted corner bay rising to a tall concave-mansard tower roof with a dormer at the right (north?) end, a one-storey columned entrance porch with arched openings and a curved roof, panelled wall surfaces, high basement and stoop; a coachman and footman in top hats on a brougham at the kerb, a gas lamp, granite curb and a rough street surface. Demolished c.1899–1900 when Glessner bought the lot, so it shows the PRE-1904 predecessor of the 1700/1706 townhouses. Page text: permits 1878 (Busby, 3-storey and basement addition, $12,000) and 1879 (two-storey barn, $3,000); the Inter Ocean (21 Nov 1879) called it "a two-story brownstone front".

images.notes: "…at 3:25 o'clock yesterday afternoon. The horses and carriages were quickly removed and were not injured. The loss on the building is estimated at $150." images.creator: Inland Architect Press (photographic plate); Burling & Whitehouse, architects
images.repository: Art Institute of Chicago, Ryerson and Burnham Archives (Archival Image Collection; Inland Architect plates, 720.5 I56)

images.rights_basis: Plate published in the US in 1890 (pre-1931); AIC record says to contact archives@artic.edu for rights information about its digital copy
images.found_via: AIC CONTENTdm API search 'mcbirney'; plate list confirmed in archive.org sim_inland-architect-and-news-record_1890-01_14_8
images.notes: New house for Hugh J. (Johnston) McBirney, the son of Hugh McBirney of 1736: a narrow three-storey rock-faced stone front with a steep front gable (oculus), Tudor-style mullioned and transomed windows with stone quoined surrounds, a carved panel over a plain square-headed entrance, brick side wall with a mansard-roofed rear wing and dormers; attached at left to a neighbour with a corner turret, carved bay and Romanesque arched entrance; at right an open side yard with picket fence; building materials on the unfinished walk. ADDRESS: AIC catalogues this as 1736 S. Prairie, but 1736 (NW corner of 18th) was the elder McBirney's Second Empire house (blog c.1890 photo; Rand McNally 1893 strip), while the 1904 Blue Book lists the Hugh J. McBirney household at 1625 Prairie, and the 'Hibbardville' map places McBirney on the east side of the 1600 block between Farwell and Forsyth. The 1911 Sanborn shows 1625 as the end of an attached group 1621–1625 ('3B; section 4'), matching the attached-left/open-right siting here. Treat as 1625 (not in the building index) pending directory confirmation; it stood in 1904. Supporting context: Inland Architect Nov. 1885 (vol. 6 no. 5, building news) reports 'Architects Treat & Foltz: For Granger Farwell, at 1625 Prairie avenue, residence, cost $11,000' and the Conzen/Knox 1886 map places Farwell at 1623 — so the turreted, Romanesque-arched house attached at the LEFT (north) of the McBirney front is probably the 1885 Farwell house, and the McBirney house the next lot south (1625 by 1904), with the open lots toward 1637 at right.

images.notes: The SAME volume and sheet as the 1911 sheet 35 already held (MAP-1911-35), but with paste-over corrections to 1950: it records what replaced each mansion (e.g. on sheet 28 the R. R. Donnelley roll-paper warehouse, Gaylord Products/Hump Hairpin factory, 'Aeronautical University', and on 20 the Railway Express garage over the Pullman/1700 east side; sheet 35 Revere Camera, Donnelley, auto sales). Use it to date demolitions (later than 1911) and to see the surviving houses' footprints re-surveyed. Later evidence only — the 1904 layer stays with the 1911 base. LoC holds no 1890s–1906 Sanborn of this area: its 1906 Vol. 1 South Division covers only the congested district north of 12th St., and the 1890s volumes it holds are Vols. 9–16 and suburbs.

Shows, 34 years after the target date: the Prairie/Calumet blocks between 16th and 22nd with many vacant lots and a few surviving mansions, the R. R. Use for street/alley geometry, lot lines and the location of surviving buildings; ~1.7 m/pixel in the crop — individual houses are blocks, not façades.
